title: Two problems in sixty minutes
objectives: Solve two medium problems inside 60 minutes, with a plan for partial credit.

screens.title: Count by remainder
screens.prose: This code is correct but slow. It passes the small groups. Make the large group pass. `ds` l7 counted subarrays with a given sum. New here: two prefix sums with the same remainder bound a subarray whose sum is divisible by `k`.

params.title: Statement
lines: k is at least 1. Return the number of non-empty subarrays whose sum is divisible by k.
Values may be negative or zero.
The starter checks every subarray: correct, but slow.

screens.question: Write a fast `count_subarrays_divisible_by_k(nums, k)`.

widget.how: Check runs 11 hidden tests: nine small ones and two of 400,000 numbers. A case that runs past 5 seconds stops the rest.

hints.text: Two prefix sums with the same remainder: what lies between them?
A subarray whose sum leaves remainder 0.
Keep a dict counting each remainder seen, starting with `{0: 1}`. Add the count of the current remainder before you increase it.

feedback.correct: Count how many earlier prefixes share each remainder.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first failing test.

byKey.test-1: Test 1: two subarrays have a sum divisible by 5.
byKey.test-2: Test 2 did not match. Trace it by hand.
byKey.test-3: Test 3: an empty list has no subarray.
byKey.test-4: Test 4: every one of the 6 subarrays of zeros counts.
byKey.test-5: Test 5: Python's `%` is never negative, so negative sums need no fix.
byKey.test-6: Test 6 did not match. Trace it by hand.
byKey.test-7: Test 7 did not match. Trace it by hand.
byKey.test-8: Test 8 did not match. Trace it by hand.
byKey.test-9: Test 9: the prefix remainders are 0, 2, 2 and 2.
byKey.test-10: Test 10: 400,000 numbers. A double loop makes 80 billion steps.
byKey.test-11: Test 11: the remainders alternate between 0 and 1.

explain.text: A prefix sum is the total so far. Two prefixes with the same remainder differ by a multiple of `k`, so each pair bounds one good subarray. Counting pairs with a dict takes one pass.

lines: Tests 1 to 9: at most 6 numbers each.

Tests 1 to 9. Tests 10 and 11 are large.

screens.title: The same count in C++
screens.prose: This code is correct but slow, and the same 11 tests apply. New in C++: `%` of a negative number is negative, so normalise the remainder.
screens.question: Write the fast version in C++.

tests.call: [&]{ std::vector<int> v; for (int i = 0; i < 200000; ++i) { v.push_back(1); v.push_back(-1); } return count_subarrays_divisible_by_k(v, 2); }()

widget.how: Check runs the same 11 tests. The result is a `long long`, as the largest count is 80,000,200,000.

hints.text: What does `-1 % 3` give in C++?
-1, not 2. The remainder keeps the sign of the sum.
Use `((total + x) % k + k) % k` so every remainder is 0 to k - 1. Keep `total` and the count in `long long`.

feedback.correct: Normalise the remainder, then count with a map.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check which test failed.

byKey.test-1: Test 1: two subarrays have a sum divisible by 5.
byKey.test-2: Test 2 did not match. Trace it by hand.
byKey.test-3: Test 3 did not match. Trace it by hand.
byKey.test-4: Test 4 did not match. Trace it by hand.
byKey.test-5: Test 5: check a negative sum against `k`.
byKey.test-6: Test 6 did not match. Trace it by hand.
byKey.test-7: Test 7 did not match. Trace it by hand.
byKey.test-8: Test 8 did not match. Trace it by hand.
byKey.test-9: Test 9: without the fix this returns 1, not 3.
byKey.test-10: Test 10: 80 billion steps for a double loop.
byKey.test-11: Test 11 needs `long long` for the count.

explain.text: A negative sum has a negative remainder in C++, so equal remainders could look different. Adding `k` and taking `%` again puts every remainder in 0 to `k - 1`. The count needs `long long` because it reaches 80,000,200,000.

screens.title: The longest zero-sum stretch
screens.prose: This code is correct but slow, like the last one. Keep a dict from each prefix sum to the first index where you saw it. When a prefix sum repeats, the stretch between the two sightings sums to zero.

params.title: Statement
lines: Return the length of the longest contiguous subarray whose sum is 0, or 0 if there is none.
Values may be negative or zero.
The starter tries every start and end: correct, but slow.

screens.question: Write a fast `longest_zero_sum_subarray(nums)`.

widget.how: Check runs 12 hidden tests: ten small ones and two of about 400,000 numbers.

hints.text: What does a repeated prefix sum tell you?
The numbers between the two sightings add to zero.
Start with `{0: -1}`. If the total is in the dict, the stretch is `i - first[total]`. Otherwise store `i`.

feedback.correct: Store the first index of each prefix sum.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first failing test.

byKey.test-1: Test 1 did not match. Trace it by hand.
byKey.test-2: Test 2 did not match. Trace it by hand.
byKey.test-3: Test 3: an empty list has no stretch.
byKey.test-4: Test 4: a single 7 does not sum to zero.
byKey.test-5: Test 5: a single 0 is a stretch of length 1.
byKey.test-6: Test 6: no stretch sums to zero, so the answer is 0.
byKey.test-7: Test 7 did not match. Trace it by hand.
byKey.test-8: Test 8: the whole list sums to 0, so the answer is 4.
byKey.test-9: Test 9 did not match. Trace it by hand.
byKey.test-10: Test 10: 400,000 numbers, and the whole list sums to zero.
byKey.test-11: Test 11: the last number spoils the whole list but not the rest.
byKey.test-12: Test 12: the zero-sum stretch starts at the second number, so the total is never 0. Use the first sighting of 10.

explain.text: Equal prefix sums mark a stretch that adds to zero. Keeping the first index of each sum makes the stretch as long as possible. One pass with a dict finds the longest.

screens.title: First or latest
screens.prose: Take `[4, -4, 3, -3]`. Its prefix sums, with the empty start, are 0, 4, 0, 3 and 0. The sum 0 is seen at index -1, at index 1 and at index 3.
screens.question: When a prefix sum repeats, which index does the dict keep?

options.text: The first sighting
The latest sighting
options.why: You overwrote the first sighting. The stretch from 1 to 3 has length 2, shorter than the whole list.

options.text: The middle sighting
options.why: You kept a sighting in the middle. Both ends of the stretch then fall short of the longest.

options.text: Both of them
options.why: You kept every sighting. One index is enough, and the earliest gives the longest stretch.

hints.text: Which start gives the longest stretch?
The earliest sighting.
From index -1 to 3 is length 4. From the latest, 1 to 3, is only 2.

feedback.correct: The first sighting gives the longest stretch: here all 4.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The earliest start is the longest.

byKey.b: You overwrote the first sighting, so the length was only 2.
byKey.c: A middle start loses length at the front.
byKey.d: Keeping every sighting wastes memory. The earliest is enough.

explain.text: The stretch runs from the first sighting to the current index. The earliest start makes it longest, so the dict never overwrites. Here the whole list, length 4, sums to zero.

screens.title: The minute plan
screens.prose:
Two medium problems fit in an hour when each has a box.

```python
# 00:00 read both, note limits, rank     (5)
# 00:05 problem 1: brute force, then fast  (25 box)
# 00:30 problem 2: brute force, then fast  (25 box)
# 00:55 tests and edge cases on both        (5)
```
